entries.root_cause: The G1 successor-authorization manifest described a proposed authorization and a post-merge effect in prose-like fields but did not encode the repository-standard machine-readable implementation_authority_before_merge and implementation_authority_after_merge transition. Automated consumers could therefore not distinguish merge permission from the implementation authority that becomes effective only after canonicalization.

The first G1 authorization validator did not attest the manifest effective_rule, allowing a manifest-only mutation to claim immediate effect while all other exact-head authorization fields remained green. A merge-gated proposal therefore lacked a permanent executable assertion for its activation rule.

The initial G1 exact-scope validator checked only a subset of explicitly_not_authorized entries. Removing an unlisted exclusion such as browser long-lived credentials, ITSM, or production C3 numerics could therefore silently widen the successor authorization while the dedicated validator stayed green.

The G1 task packet delegated repository path selection to the later implementation PR, so post-merge implementation authority had a bounded capability but no pre-reviewed machine-readable file boundary. That allowed a future implementation to self-classify shared runtime, authority, contract, or governance paths as G1-specific without successor authorization.

The base learning resolver credited newly registered G1 falsifiers from entrypoint reachability alone. Without registering G1's must_fail helper in the strict falsifier-effects layer, a credited G1 function could be reduced to a no-op body while retaining its name and main-call shape, leaving the ledger apparently guarded.

The authorization manifest declared that future implementation diffs must obey the G1 path policy, but no canonical-base/exact-head workflow actually consumed that policy against a future implementation PR's complete diff. A mixed G1/shared-core PR could therefore violate the reviewed boundary without an executable gate.

The strict falsifier-effects registry verified that credited G1 falsifiers called a helper named must_fail, but did not execute that helper against both rejected and accepted mutations. The helper body itself could therefore be replaced by a no-op while every name/reachability check remained green.

The first future-G1 scope workflow executed the evaluator from the candidate PR HEAD. A candidate could therefore replace the workflow or validator that judged its own diff, converting the enforcement boundary into self-attestation.

The first G1 relevance rule inferred implementation intent only from a voluntary branch prefix or allowed G1 path. A candidate using an unrecognized branch and only shared-core changes could avoid classification, so omission of identifying metadata did not fail closed.

The executable implementation-diff finding was reconciled to a manifest-policy falsifier rather than a probe that exercised the actual Git diff gate. The real scope falsifier therefore could weaken while the ledger still reported the finding as guarded.

Materializing a validator from the trusted base was insufficient because the pull_request workflow orchestration that decided whether to invoke it still came from candidate-controlled workflow content. A candidate could remove or replace the trusted-validator call before the base-owned evaluator ever ran.

The temporary authorization bootstrap was keyed only to an old base SHA, branch name and repository identity, making the exception reusable through another PR aimed at the historical base. A supposedly one-time bypass therefore remained representable after canonicalization.

The second G1 relevance rule still allowed a PR with noncanonical branch, no label, no claim and only forbidden shared-core changes to return not-g1 before metadata or path enforcement. Voluntary metadata therefore still controlled whether the guard ran at all.

The trusted default-branch issue_comment caller still accepted the pull request base SHA from any writable base branch. Because it materialized the evaluator from that base object, a contributor able to control a nondefault base branch could supply the supposedly trusted Python evaluator while the caller itself remained default-branch owned.

The issue_comment scope attestation ran on default-branch workflow identity but did not publish its result to the resolved implementation PR head. A successful or failed run therefore could not be required as a stable head-associated status and would not automatically become stale when the candidate HEAD changed.

The ledger credited the outer G1 scope-gate falsifier while strict learning verified only unrelated direct must_fail calls. Individual delegated scope probes could therefore be replaced by pass without losing ledger credit, including the all-voluntary-metadata omission guard that represented a material bypass.

A successful G1 scope status could outlive the exact default-branch base it evaluated, so the same implementation HEAD could retain stale green evidence after the default branch advanced. Automatic push invalidation was considered but is not authoritative because GitHub Actions push workflows may be skipped. The systemic resolution is therefore live source-authenticated readiness: an independent trusted issue_comment command re-reads the current default-branch tip and rejects any scope evidence whose encoded base no longer equals that tip.

A stable commit-status context identified the intended G1 scope evidence but did not authenticate who published it. Another same-repository principal with status-write authority could publish a look-alike success under the same context, so context plus state was not sufficient provenance for a security-sensitive readiness decision.

The attempted stale-base guard depended on a push-triggered invalidation workflow. GitHub Actions skip directives can suppress push workflows, so a default-branch commit containing a skip directive could advance the trusted base without running the invalidator and leave the old implementation-head status green.

The required G1 PR label was checked when attestation coordinates were first resolved, but labels are mutable without changing the implementation HEAD. Removing the label afterward could therefore leave prior success evidence green unless current label state was re-read at readiness and final merge preflight.

The first base-advance finding was credited to a probe that asserted workflow marker strings rather than executing the invalidation semantics. A behavior-changing mutation inside the marker-preserving workflow could therefore bypass the intended guard while the ledger still reported executable coverage.
